content: I wonder if we can extend the moment of inertia thing as well. Once they've found the moment of inertia, what else could they do?

We could feed into some sort of dynamics, for eg. pendulums, rolling cylinders - you could combine the derived I with other lemmas like parallel axis theorem and stuff to figure out/prove formulas for time period, force etc.

Thinking in terms of the experience itself for students, maybe we need a standard format for a file with different dynamics examples. Then we start with deriving the moment of inertia, and then have it similar to natural numbers games, proving lemmas and results and then it ends with a PR to physlib
Have not fully fleshed out the above ideas, I'm still thinking exactly how this would work - maybe we should start another thread

It reminds me of an exam question on rigid bodies I once put to grad students: a rigid ball is rolling without slipping on an infinite turn table, describe the motion and draw parallels with an electromagnetic phenomenon. Being able to work this out in physlib would be a good demonstration of having all tools for eom development for rigid bodies.
